prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN)   -- Mexicans in the United States sent home 12.2 percent less money this past August than the same month last year, the Banco de Mexico said Wednesday. Mexicans in the U.S. are sending fewer dollars home and are suffering from a tough economy. That translates into remittances of $1.9 billion, versus $2.2 billion last year, said the bank, which blamed tough economic times in the United States for the decline. "The prolonged deceleration of economic activity in the United States has adversely affected the opportunities for employment in that country and, consequently, those of the Mexican migrants," the bank said in a statement posted on its Web site. August's tally quickens a trend -- during the first eight months of the year, remittances fell 4 percent to $15.6 billion, the statement said. The numbers translate easily into stories of hardship. Marilyn Pena lives outside Mexico City and depends on remittances to get by. Her father migrated to Chicago 12 years ago to find work and, in good months, sends his daughter about $200 per week. But last week he sent nothing. "He told me he has no more work because of the situation there," Pena said. "Temporary workers are always the first to lose their jobs in crises like this one," said Luis Pena, an economist. "Since many Mexicans in the United States are there illegally, they are most vulnerable to unemployment." Some economists predict the drop will increase by year's end to 20 percent. After oil exports, remittances are Mexico's second-largest source of foreign currency. In Atlanta, Georgia, which has one of the greatest concentrations of Mexican residents in the southeastern United States, Yasmin Gutierrez runs a company that Mexican immigrants use to send dollars abroad. "Before, they used to come every week and they used to send big amounts and lately, well, nothing, or almost nothing. Some clients are no longer coming, and those that are coming are sending small amounts." Rosina Gonzalez, who ran a Western Union office in Atlanta several years ago and recently returned to the job, said she has noticed a big change. Back then, "everyone was sending money to Mexico, Mexico, Mexico -- a lot of money," she said. "Now, I'm returning to work after four or five years and the norm now is that the people who used to send money to Mexico are asking the people in Mexico to send money here." Some are abandoning their hope for a slice of the American dream by opting to return to their country. The woman running the foreign-currency exchange service Afex, also in Atlanta, said business is so bad she is afraid of losing her job. CNN's Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to this story.

**MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) —** Mexicans living in the United States sent 12.2 percent less money home this past August than they did during the same month last year, Banco de Mexico said Wednesday.

The decline reflects the economic hardships facing Mexicans in the United States, who are sending fewer dollars home. Remittances totaled $1.9 billion, down from $2.2 billion last year, according to the bank, which attributed the decrease to difficult economic conditions in the United States.

“The prolonged deceleration of economic activity in the United States has adversely affected the opportunities for employment in that country and, consequently, those of the Mexican migrants,” the bank said in a statement posted on its website.

August’s figures indicate an accelerating trend. During the first eight months of the year, remittances fell 4 percent to $15.6 billion, the statement said.

Behind those numbers are stories of hardship. Marilyn Pena, who lives outside Mexico City, depends on remittances to make ends meet. Her father migrated to Chicago 12 years ago in search of work and, in good months, sends his daughter about $200 a week. Last week, however, he sent nothing.

“He told me he has no more work because of the situation there,” Pena said.

“Temporary workers are always the first to lose their jobs in crises like this one,” said economist Luis Pena. “Since many Mexicans in the United States are there illegally, they are most vulnerable to unemployment.”

Some economists predict the decline will reach 20 percent by the end of the year.

After oil exports, remittances are Mexico’s second-largest source of foreign currency.

In Atlanta, Georgia, home to one of the largest concentrations of Mexican residents in the southeastern United States, Yasmin Gutierrez runs a company that Mexican immigrants use to send dollars abroad.

“Before, they used to come every week and they used to send big amounts and lately, well, nothing, or almost nothing,” she said. “Some clients are no longer coming, and those that are coming are sending small amounts.”

Rosina Gonzalez, who managed a Western Union office in Atlanta several years ago and recently returned to the job, said she has noticed a significant change.

Back then, “everyone was sending money to Mexico, Mexico, Mexico — a lot of money,” she said. “Now, I’m returning to work after four or five years and the norm now is that the people who used to send money to Mexico are asking the people in Mexico to send money here.”

Some are giving up their hopes of securing a piece of the American dream and choosing to return to their home country.

The woman who runs the foreign-currency exchange service Afex, also in Atlanta, said business is so poor that she fears losing her job.

CNN’s Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to this report.

**MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) —** Money transfers from Mexicans living in the United States declined sharply in August, as the weakening U.S. economy reduced employment opportunities for migrant workers.

Banco de Mexico reported Wednesday that August remittances totaled $1.9 billion, down 12.2 percent from the $2.2 billion sent during the same month a year earlier. The central bank attributed the decrease to difficult economic conditions in the United States.

In a statement published on its website, the bank said the extended slowdown in U.S. economic activity had limited employment prospects generally and had therefore also reduced job opportunities for Mexican migrants.

The August figures marked an acceleration of an existing decline. During the first eight months of the year, remittances dropped 4 percent to $15.6 billion, according to the bank.

For families dependent on money from relatives abroad, those statistics represent real financial hardship. Marilyn Pena, who lives near Mexico City, relies on funds sent by her father. He moved to Chicago 12 years ago in search of work and sends her roughly $200 a week when employment is steady. The previous week, however, he sent no money.

Pena said her father explained that the economic situation in the United States had left him without work.

Economist Luis Pena said temporary employees are typically the first to be dismissed during an economic crisis. He added that many Mexicans living in the United States lack legal status, making them especially susceptible to unemployment.

Some economists expect the year-over-year decline in remittances to reach 20 percent by the end of the year. The transfers are Mexico’s second-biggest source of foreign currency, surpassed only by oil exports.

The downturn is also evident in Atlanta, Georgia, home to one of the largest Mexican populations in the southeastern United States. Yasmin Gutierrez operates a business that helps Mexican immigrants transfer dollars overseas. She said customers once visited weekly and sent substantial sums, but recently they have sent little or nothing. Some clients have stopped coming altogether, while those who still use the service are transferring smaller amounts.

Rosina Gonzalez, who managed an Atlanta Western Union office several years ago and has recently returned to that work, said conditions have changed dramatically. Four or five years earlier, she recalled, customers regularly sent large amounts to Mexico. Now, she said, many former senders are instead asking relatives in Mexico to transfer money to them in the United States.

Some migrants are also giving up their pursuit of the American dream and choosing to return to Mexico.

At Afex, an Atlanta foreign-currency exchange service, the woman in charge said business had deteriorated so severely that she feared losing her job.

CNN’s Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on how the U.S. economic slowdown is reducing employment among Mexican migrants and cutting the amount of money they send home to their families.
counterfactuals.output:
## U.S. Slowdown Hits Mexican Migrant Jobs and Remittances

A slowdown in the U.S. economy reduces employment among Mexican migrants because many work in industries that contract quickly when growth weakens—particularly construction, hospitality, restaurants, manufacturing, landscaping, and other labor-intensive services. Undocumented workers are especially vulnerable because they often have temporary jobs, limited employment protections, and little access to unemployment benefits.

As employers cut hours, postpone projects, or lay off workers, migrants have less money available after paying for rent, food, transportation, and other U.S. expenses. Some also struggle to find replacement jobs because several migrant-heavy industries may be weakening at the same time. Workers may remain in the United States rather than return to Mexico, but send money home less frequently or in smaller amounts.

The resulting decline in remittances directly affects families in Mexico. These transfers commonly pay for food, housing, medical care, education, utilities, and small businesses. The impact is often strongest in rural communities and states with long histories of migration, where remittances represent an important part of household income and local economic activity.

Lower transfers can have broader effects: families reduce consumption, delay home construction, withdraw children from school, or take on debt. Local shops and service providers then lose business, spreading the effects beyond households that receive remittances. Mexican banks and money-transfer companies may also process fewer transactions.

Exchange-rate movements can partly cushion the decline. If the Mexican peso weakens against the dollar, each dollar sent home buys more pesos. However, that benefit may not offset a substantial fall in migrants’ employment, working hours, or wages.

Overall, the U.S. slowdown is transmitted to Mexico through the labor market: fewer jobs and shorter hours for migrants lead to smaller remittances, weakening household finances and economic activity in migrant-sending communities.

counterfactuals.output:
**Mexico remittances fall as U.S. slowdown squeezes migrant workers**

**MEXICO CITY —** Money sent home by Mexicans living abroad dropped to about $1.9 billion in August from $2.2 billion a year earlier, reflecting weakening U.S. employment and growing financial pressure on migrant families.

The roughly 14% decline was driven largely by conditions in the United States, the source of most remittances to Mexico. Mexican migrants are heavily represented in construction, manufacturing, hospitality and other industries hit by the housing downturn and slowing economy. As jobs disappeared and working hours were reduced, migrants had less money available after paying for rent, food and transportation.

Tighter immigration enforcement and increased workplace checks also likely contributed. Undocumented workers facing deportation or difficulty finding employment may move less frequently, accept lower wages or keep more cash on hand for emergencies.

For migrant workers, the fall underscores a difficult tradeoff. Many continue sending money even when their own earnings decline, cutting personal expenses or taking additional jobs to support relatives. But prolonged unemployment can force them to reduce the size or frequency of transfers.

The consequences are immediate in Mexico, where remittances help millions of households pay for food, housing, school fees, health care and utilities. Rural communities and poorer states with limited formal employment are especially dependent on the payments. A sustained decline could weaken local consumption and push some families to borrow, postpone medical treatment or seek new sources of income.

Mexico’s economy as a whole is less dependent on remittances than some smaller Latin American countries, but the transfers remain an important source of foreign currency and household support. The decline also removes a cushion just as higher prices and slower economic growth are straining family budgets.

Remittance companies, banks and money-transfer shops face lower transaction volumes and fee revenue. Businesses may respond by cutting charges, offering better exchange rates or expanding mobile and bank-account transfers to compete for customers. Smaller agents in migrant neighborhoods and Mexican towns could be hit hardest because they rely heavily on transfer commissions and related foot traffic.

The August figures suggest that remittances are no longer insulated from the broader U.S. downturn. If employment conditions continue to deteriorate, both migrants and the relatives who depend on them are likely to face further pressure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed wire-service report on the financial crisis’s impact on Mexican immigrants in the United States, noting falling remittances, layoffs among temporary and undocumented workers, and Mexico’s dependence on remittances as a source of foreign currency.
counterfactuals.output:
**Financial crisis cuts jobs, remittances for Mexican immigrants in United States**

**LOS ANGELES, March 2009 (Wire Service)** — The global financial crisis is hitting Mexican immigrants in the United States on two fronts, eliminating jobs in industries that rely heavily on foreign labor while reducing the money sent to families in Mexico.

Mexican workers—especially temporary employees and undocumented immigrants—have been particularly exposed to layoffs because many are concentrated in construction, manufacturing, hotels, restaurants, landscaping and other industries that contracted sharply during the recession. Their losses are being felt far beyond the U.S. labor market: remittances are a major source of household income in Mexico and one of the country’s largest sources of foreign currency.

The collapse of the U.S. housing market dealt an early blow. Construction had provided relatively well-paid work to large numbers of Mexican migrants, including many without legal status. As residential projects were canceled and contractors cut payrolls, workers who lacked seniority, formal contracts or unemployment insurance were often among the first dismissed.

The downturn then spread to factories and service businesses. Temporary workers, day laborers and employees paid off the books faced reduced hours or abrupt layoffs, frequently without severance pay. Undocumented migrants generally cannot claim unemployment benefits, even when payroll taxes have been deducted from their wages, and many are reluctant to seek public assistance because they fear immigration enforcement or jeopardizing relatives.

Mexico’s central bank said remittances fell to about **$25.1 billion in 2008**, a decline of roughly **3.6 percent** from the previous year and the first annual decrease since the bank began tracking the transfers systematically. The decline accelerated late in the year as the U.S. recession deepened and the unemployment rate climbed.

The fall has broad implications for Mexico. Remittances have ranked alongside oil exports, manufacturing and tourism as a crucial generator of foreign currency. They also flow directly to households, making them particularly important in rural communities and poorer states such as Michoacán, Guanajuato, Zacatecas, Oaxaca and Guerrero, where migration to the United States has long supplemented limited local employment.

Families typically use the money for food, housing, school fees, medicine and utility bills rather than investment. Even a small reduction can therefore have an immediate effect on consumption and living standards. In towns where a large share of residents depend on relatives abroad, declining transfers also hurt shops, transport operators and construction workers.

The pressure does not necessarily mean that migrants will return to Mexico in large numbers. Returning can be expensive and risky, particularly for undocumented workers who may be unable to cross the border again. Many have spouses or U.S.-born children in the United States, and employment prospects in Mexico have also weakened as exports and industrial production decline.

Instead, migrant households are adopting a range of survival strategies. Some workers are moving between states in search of agricultural or service jobs. Others are taking lower wages, sharing housing, postponing medical care or sending smaller amounts home. In some cases, migrants are continuing to remit money by cutting their own spending, a pattern that can delay—but not prevent—the impact of unemployment on relatives in Mexico.

Workers admitted under temporary visa programs face a different set of risks. Their legal status is often tied to a specific employer, leaving them with limited ability to change jobs after layoffs or reductions in hours. Undocumented workers are even more vulnerable to wage theft and unsafe conditions because filing a complaint may expose them to retaliation or scrutiny of their immigration status.

The peso’s depreciation against the dollar has provided a partial cushion. Each dollar sent to Mexico buys more pesos, allowing some families to maintain local purchasing power despite receiving fewer dollars. But economists say that benefit is offset by higher prices for imported goods, weaker employment and broader economic uncertainty.

The remittance decline also poses a policy challenge for the Mexican government. Unlike export earnings or foreign investment, remittances are private transfers and cannot be directed by the state. Yet they support millions of households and help finance local consumption. A prolonged fall would increase pressure on social programs and on regions already suffering from poverty and limited access to formal credit.

For the United States, the crisis underscores the precarious position of immigrant labor. During the economic expansion, Mexican migrants filled jobs in fast-growing sectors and helped meet demand for flexible labor. During the contraction, that flexibility has translated into rapid job losses and little protection.

The eventual course of remittances will depend heavily on the U.S. labor market. A recovery in construction, manufacturing and hospitality could stabilize transfers, but continued unemployment among Hispanic and immigrant workers would deepen the decline. Until then, the recession will continue to cross the border with every paycheck lost—and every money transfer reduced or canceled.
